{{smaller block|No man would say at what time of the night the ship (in case she was steering our course) might ''forge ahead'' of us, or how near she might be when she passed.
{{right|''Dickens.''}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') To move ahead, as in coming to anchor after the sails are furled.—'''To get ahead, hold ahead,''' etc. See ''get'', ''hold'', etc.—'''To run ahead of one’s reckoning.''' See ''reckoning''.}}

'''aheap''' (ạ-hēp′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.''  [< ''a''<sup>3</sup>, on, in, + ''heap''.]  In a heap; in a huddled or crouching condition, as from terror; in a constrained attitude, as from fear or astonishment: as, this fearful sight struck us all ''aheap'' (= all of a heap).
{{smaller block|<poem>When some fresh bruit
Startled me all ''aheap!'' and soon I saw
The horridest shape that ever raised my awe.</poem>
{{right|''Hood'', Mids. Fairies, xvi.}}}}

'''aheight†''' (ạ-hīt′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.''  [Also spelled ''ahight''; < ''a''<sup>3</sup>, on, + ''height'', ''hight''. Cf. ''aloft'', of similar sense.]  Aloft; on high: as, “look up ''a-height'',” ''Shak.'', Lear, iv. 6.

'''ahem''' (ạ-hem′), ''interj.''  [Intended to represent an inarticulate sound made in clearing the throat, usually as preparatory to speaking.]  An utterance designed to attract attention, express doubt, etc.

'''ahight†''' (ạ-hī′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.''  [< ''a''<sup>3</sup>, on, + ''high''.]  On high. {{smaller block|One heav’d ''a-high'', to be hurl’d down below.
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., iv. 4.}}}}

'''ahint, ahin''' (a-hint′, a-hin′), ''prep.'' or ''adv.''  [< ME. ''at hind'', < AS. ''æt-hindan'', behind, < ''æt'', E. ''at'', + ''hindan'', from the back, behind: see ''a-''<sup>7</sup>, ''hind''<sup>3</sup>, ''behind'', and cf. ''afore''.]  Behind. [Scotch.]

'''ahm''' (äm), ''n.'' Same as ''aam''.

'''ahna-tree''' (ä′nä̤-trē), ''n.''  [< ''ahna'', ''anna'', native name, + ''tree''.]  A large evergreen thorny species of ''Acacia'', growing abundantly in the sandy river-beds of Damaraland, Africa. {{smaller|The wood is light but durable, and the bark is said to be a good tanning material. The tree bears a profusion of pods, which are very nutritious food for cattle, and are also eaten by the natives. Also written ''anna-tree''.}}

'''ahold†''' (a-hōld′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' or ''a.''  [< ''a''<sup>3</sup>, on, + ''hold''.]  Near the wind, so as to hold or keep to it: as, to lay a ship ''a-hold''.  ''Shak.''

'''ahoy''' (ạ-hoi′), ''interj.''  [Same as ''hoy'', ''interj.'', with prefix ''a-'' marking a slight preliminary utterance: see ''a-''<sup>9</sup>.]  ''Naut.'', an exclamation used to attract the attention of persons at a distance: as, ship ''ahoy!''

'''ahu''' (ä′hö), ''n.''  [Pers. ''āhū'', a deer.]  One of the native names of the common gazel of central Asia, the ''Gazella subgutturosa'' (''Antilope subgutturosa'' of Güldenstädt). {{smaller|It is said to inhabit in herds the open country of central Asia, Persia, the Baikal region, and to be found from the eastern boundary of Bokhara to the Hellespont. Its principal food is a species of wormwood, ''Artemisia Pontica''. The ahu is pale-brown, white}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
